title: Why splitting the bill makes everyone pay more
description:
When six people split the bill evenly, a $12 dessert costs you only $2: your friends pay the other $10. But everyone does the same math, so six desserts arrive and your share is $12 anyway. In a 2004 restaurant experiment in Haifa with tables of six strangers, diners paying their own spent 37 shekels on average, diners splitting evenly 51 (over a third more), and diners eating for free 82. Asked beforehand, 4 in 5 said they would rather pay their own.

Numbers checked in code (verify.py) from the paper's table of every diner's bill. Source: Gneezy, Haruvy & Yafe, The Inefficiency of Splitting the Bill, The Economic Journal (2004).

beats.say: Economists tested this in a restaurant in Israel, with tables of six strangers. Paying their own, they spent 37 shekels each. Splitting, 51. Free, 82.
And before ordering, 4 out of 5 said they'd rather pay their own.
Splitting doesn't share the cost. It shares the temptation. Pay your own, and the table spends a quarter less.
